tags.gist: Says the paper dwells on model performance and monitoring but neglects how devices are operated, secured, maintained, repaired, calibrated and retired.
Lists priorities: safe operation during dependency failures, GenAI cybersecurity, serviceability, lifecycle support, dependency transparency, calibration, ownership, fleet risk and service personnel.
Wants sponsors to map which functions depend on cloud, model or identity services and to test behavior under each failure, with a validated fallback state.
Wants dependence on connectivity, and how fast harm follows an outage, treated as risk modifiers.
Wants cybersecurity evaluation to go beyond prompt injection to supply-chain, poisoned retrieval, compromised tools and privileged access, with manufacturers accountable for chosen dependencies.
Wants a serviceability and lifecycle plan so hospital technicians and independent servicers have the documentation, diagnostics, calibration tools and access to maintain equipment.
Wants lifecycle planning for dependency-driven obsolescence, with disclosed support commitments, end-of-support notice, migration plans and local or non-AI fallback where appropriate.
Wants AI calibration distinguished from biomedical calibration, since neither benchmarking nor sensor calibration alone shows a changed model reads measurements safely.
Wants fleet-level common-mode risk considered, since one shared model, cloud or identity dependency can disable an entire device class at once.
Wants benchmarking elements added for cybersecurity and dependency integrity, operational resilience, and maintainability and lifecycle support.
Wants healthcare technology management, biomedical technicians, clinical engineers, cybersecurity staff and independent servicers explicitly included in the discussion.
Says a complete lifecycle framework must ask whether organizations can safely operate, secure, maintain, repair, calibrate, recover, update and retire the device.
Calls the paper a useful start that does not yet address whether products stay safe, available, secure and serviceable after deployment, especially inside equipment.
Wants validated continuity and safe, obvious failure during loss of network, cloud, model or external dependencies.
Wants GenAI-specific cybersecurity and dependency-integrity requirements spanning the model, data, API, tool, identity, update and service supply chain.
Wants maintainability and qualified repair access preserved so organizations are not responsible for availability without the means to maintain devices.
Wants lifecycle-support commitments so withdrawal of support by an OEM, cloud or model provider does not strand functional equipment.
Wants end-to-end calibration and return-to-service verification that links physical, software, model and clinical-output checks.
Wants fleet-level, common-mode and third-party concentration risk evaluated, since one provider or update can hit many facilities and manufacturers.
Wants operational and lifecycle risks made measurable elements of risk assessment, benchmarking, labeling and monitoring, not procurement afterthoughts.
Wants technology management, clinical engineering, cybersecurity and service stakeholders given a defined part in building and monitoring the framework.
Requests three new elements: cybersecurity and dependency integrity, operational resilience and continuity, and maintainability and lifecycle support.
Wants connectivity dependence, time-to-harm during outages, fallback capability and common-mode exposure treated as risk modifiers.
Warns that addressing only the GenAI component leaves out system-level safety such as downtime behavior, service access, calibration and end-of-life support.
Wants device behavior defined and validated under every dependency loss, from internet and model API outages to identity failures, with proportionate fallback requirements.
Wants connectivity dependency, dependency criticality, detectability of degradation, downstream safeguards and time-to-harm as explicit modifiers in the risk framework.
Wants a cybersecurity benchmarking element covering model compromise, retrieval poisoning, tool and API compromise and supply-chain attacks, with a system threat model.
Wants a required serviceability plan giving qualified personnel manuals, diagnostics, logs, calibration procedures, parts information and a controlled local service pathway.
Wants enforceable lifecycle-support disclosures and transition plans for when a provider retires a model, API or service, including escrow or continuity mechanisms.
Wants verification of the full measurement-to-output chain defined after maintenance, part replacement, model or prompt changes and migrations, beyond AI benchmarks.
Wants sponsors to assess shared-dependency failures that can disable whole fleets across facilities and manufacturers, including failover and staged rollout.
Wants proof of a response plan for fleet-wide common-mode failures, and wants significant service outages reported postmarket for widely deployed products.
Proposes elements S.4, R.3 and R.4 with core questions and minimum evidence for dependency integrity, resilience under outages, and serviceability.
Wants the risk framework to weigh connectivity dependence, time-to-harm, fallback, detectability, reversibility of incomplete actions, fleet size and remaining support life.
Wants monitoring to include service interruptions, security incidents, degraded-mode time, failed updates, repair delays, service retirements and fleet events.
Says ecosystem roles must not diffuse manufacturer accountability for dependencies the manufacturer selected.
Says supervisory agents cannot be the only safeguard when they share the device's model, cloud, network or identity dependencies.
Suggests master files also carry support and deprecation policies, version-pinning options, notification commitments, data portability and provider-exit arrangements.
Wants technology management, biomedical, clinical engineering, cybersecurity and service personnel consulted, since they hold practical evidence on serviceability and downtime.
Concludes the framework must cover owning, operating, securing, maintaining, repairing, recovering, updating and retiring the complete product, with clear manufacturer accountability.
